verses.text: Yahweh’s word came also to me, saying,
“You shall not take a wife, neither shall you have sons or daughters, in this place.”

For Yahweh says concerning the sons and concerning the daughters who are born in this place, and concerning their mothers who bore them, and concerning their fathers who became their father in this land:

“They shall die grievous deaths: they shall not be lamented, neither shall they be buried; they shall be as dung on the surface of the ground; and they shall be consumed by the sword, and by famine; and their dead bodies shall be food for the birds of the sky, and for the animals of the earth.”

For Yahweh says, “Don’t enter into the house of mourning, neither go to lament, neither bemoan them; for I have taken away my peace from this people,” says Yahweh, “even loving kindness and tender mercies.
Both great and small shall die in this land; they shall not be buried, neither shall men lament for them, nor cut themselves, nor make themselves bald for them;
neither shall men break bread for them in mourning, to comfort them for the dead; neither shall men give them the cup of consolation to drink for their father or for their mother.
“You shall not go into the house of feasting to sit with them, to eat and to drink.”

For Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel says: “Behold, I will cause to cease out of this place, before your eyes and in your days, the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride.

It shall happen, when you shall show this people all these words, and they ask you, ‘Why has Yahweh pronounced all this great evil against us?’ or ‘What is our iniquity? or ‘What is our sin that we have committed against Yahweh our God?’

Then you shall tell them, ‘Because your fathers have forsaken me,’ says Yahweh, ‘and have walked after other gods, and have served them, and have worshiped them, and have forsaken me, and have not kept my law;
and you have done evil more than your fathers; for, behold, you walk every one after the stubbornness of his evil heart, so that you don’t listen to me.
Therefore will I cast you out of this land into the land that you have not known, neither you nor your fathers; and there you shall serve other gods day and night; for I will show you no favor.’
“Therefore behold, the days come,” says Yahweh, “that it shall no more be said, ‘As Yahweh lives, who brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt;’

but, ‘As Yahweh lives, who brought up the children of Israel from the land of the north, and from all the countries where he had driven them.’ I will bring them again into their land that I gave to their fathers.

“Behold, I will send for many fishermen,” says Yahweh, “and they shall fish them up; and afterward I will send for many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain, and from every hill, and out of the clefts of the rocks.
For my eyes are on all their ways; they are not hidden from my face, neither is their iniquity concealed from my eyes.
First I will recompense their iniquity and their sin double, because they have polluted my land with the carcasses of their detestable things, and have filled my inheritance with their abominations.”

Yahweh, my strength, and my stronghold, and my refuge in the day of affliction, to you shall the nations come from the ends of the earth, and shall say, “Our fathers have inherited nothing but lies, vanity and things in which there is no profit.
Shall a man make to himself gods, which yet are no gods?”
“Therefore behold, I will cause them to know, this once will I cause them to know my hand and my might; and they shall know that my name is Yahweh.”

footnotes.content: The Lord speaks directly to Jeremiah—not in riddles or visions, but plainly. When God wants to teach His prophet something costly, He begins with a clear word. Even hard obedience is rooted in the intimacy of being heard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah is told not to marry, not to have children—a sign to a nation that was failing its covenant. The prophet himself becomes the message. How strange the Lord's love: asking His messenger to sacrifice what others hold most dear, so the people might finally see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord names the families—sons, daughters, mothers, fathers. This isn't abstract ruin; it is personal, generational collapse. But note: the Lord Himself speaks what will come. In naming it, He remains present to it, not absent from it. His word runs through all of it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The imagery is terrible—bodies unburied, eaten by birds and beasts. Yet even here, the Lord is the speaker. These horrors are not beyond His gaze or sovereignty. In exile, Judah will learn that even in the valley of the shadow, Yahweh has not turned away His face.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah is forbidden to comfort the mourners—even to attend funerals. The Lord has withdrawn His peace and tender mercy from the people. What a mysterious withdrawal: it is judgment, yet also an invitation to return. When mercy is hidden, it becomes precious to those who seek it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ancient mourning rites—not being buried, not lamented, not cut or shaved in grief—these customs honored the dead and knit communities. To lose them is to lose shared sorrow, to die twice. Judah's breaking of covenant severs even the bonds that survive death.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Breaking bread and sharing the cup of consolation—these were ancient acts of covenant meals and deep friendship. Their absence signals the severing of all fellowship. Yet the Lord's silence here is not eternal. One day His table will be opened again, and the cup passed freely.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No weddings, no feasts—the joyful gatherings that mark a living people are forbidden. Jeremiah walks alone, a living sign that joy has left the land. Yet in his solitude, he remains faithful to the One who called him to bear witness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The silence of joy is the deepest consequence of broken covenant. No laughter of bride and groom, no merriment among the people. Yahweh of Armies speaks: He alone can cause gladness to cease, and He alone can restore it. This is the weight of choosing idols over the living God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people will ask, 'Why?' This question marks them—they have ears to hear prophecy but not hearts to repent before judgment falls. Their confusion will be genuine; they will not understand what they have done. Yet the why is about to be answered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Your fathers forsook Me—the refrain echoes through Jeremiah's ministry. Idolatry is generational; it is learned and passed down. Yet Jeremiah is called to break the chain, to announce that the debt will be paid, that grace waits on the other side of judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You have done evil more than your fathers. Each generation chooses, and Judah's choice is their own—not inherited inevitably, but chosen stubbornly. 'You don't listen to me,' the Lord says. To refuse to hear is to refuse to turn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Exile to a land they do not know—yet not abandoned. They shall serve other gods there, and find no favor. But exile is not the end; it is a passage, a discipline. In Babylon, Israel will learn that Yahweh's name is still holy, still calling them home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A strange word: 'That shall no more be said.' The exodus from Egypt—the great deliverance—will fade from their lips. A new salvation is coming, greater still. The Lord never runs out of mercies. Each generation meets Him freshly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From the land of the north—from exile—the Lord will gather them again. What seemed like an end becomes a beginning. The Lord's promise to Abraham stands. Even in the valley of exile, the Lord says 'I will bring them again.' His faithfulness never ceases.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fishermen and hunters—both images drawn from the ancient chase, from the gathering of scattered prey. The Lord uses all means to gather His people home. Even in judgment's pursuit, His intent is recovery. The hunter's net and the fisherman's hook aim toward restoration.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: My eyes are on all their ways—nothing is hidden from the Lord. This is both threat and comfort. The people cannot escape His gaze, but neither are they ever truly forgotten. To be known utterly by God is to be held.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Double recompense for their iniquity and sin—the land itself has been defiled by their idols. The Lord takes His inheritance seriously. Yet even judgment spoken from a throne of justice is the speech of One who will not let His beloved go forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nations shall come to Yahweh and say, 'Our fathers inherited lies.' In exile, this voice emerges—Jeremiah's own cry. He addresses the Lord as his strength and stronghold. Even the prophet himself trembles, seeking shelter in the God he announces to a deaf people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shall a man make gods which are no gods? The question is rhetorical, urgent—the answer is no, and yet the people do it anyway. Idolatry is the worship of what cannot save. In the midst of exile, this question becomes the path back to truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This once will I cause them to know My hand and My might. Readers today hear an echo: the Lord's demonstrations of power and tenderness still turn hearts toward His name. In every exile of our own—grief, failure, doubt—the Lord speaks plainly: I will make Myself known again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
